```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(RdistNN)
```

`clate_dnn()` estimates a conditional local average treatment effect from
externally supplied nuisance predictions. This supported workflow uses
a binary instrument `A` and binary treatment `D`. For example, an
encouragement may change participation without determining it perfectly.
Under the IV assumptions, the target is the effect among people whose
treatment changes with encouragement, conditional on a reporting profile.

The full adjustment vector \(V=(X,Z)\) contains the pre-instrument
covariates needed for instrument exogeneity. Reporting uses only \(X\).
The effect therefore averages over the distribution of the additional
controls \(Z\) at each reporting profile, with compliance weights.
It generally differs from population CATE.

Causal interpretation requires consistency, exclusion, conditional
instrument independence given \(V\), monotonicity, instrument overlap
and positive local compliance. Without those causal assumptions, the
calculation estimates a standardized observed-data Wald functional wherever
its denominator is nonzero. Predictions alone do not verify identification.

## An example with known nuisance functions

`clate_demo_data()` generates a bounded model with endogenous treatment,
a conditionally valid instrument and known nuisance functions. The latent
compliance rank also affects untreated outcomes. Its default data frame
contains observed variables and explicitly labelled oracle prediction
columns; latent variables are available only with `keep_latent = TRUE`.

```{r data}
demo <- clate_demo_data(n = 120, seed = 20261017, heterogeneous = TRUE)
d <- demo$data
X <- as.matrix(d[c("X1", "X2")])
targets <- rbind(c(.25, .25), c(.5, .5), c(.75, .75))
data.frame(targets,
           CLATE = demo$truth$theta(targets), CATE = demo$truth$cate(targets))
```

With `heterogeneous = TRUE`, CLATE exceeds CATE by \(3/1024\).
The default model instead has the same treatment effect for everyone at a
given \(X\), so the targets coincide. Neither model turns a single
draw's confidence interval into evidence of repeated-sampling coverage.

The five prediction vectors have the following roles:

| Argument | Function evaluated at each observed \(V_i\) |
| --- | --- |
| `e` | \(P(A=1\mid V)\), instrument propensity |
| `m_y0`, `m_y1` | \(E[Y\mid A=0,V]\), \(E[Y\mid A=1,V]\) |
| `m_d0`, `m_d1` | \(E[D\mid A=0,V]\), \(E[D\mid A=1,V]\) |

Arm indices refer to the instrument. The outcome regressions do not
condition on participation as an extra control. In an application, supply
aligned predictions from the chosen learning procedure. One full-sample
nuisance state can contain five fitted regressions. The `training` label
records their provenance; it does not train or validate them.

## Matrix inputs and the two augmented signals

```{r matrix-fit}
fit <- clate_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A,
  e = d$e_oracle, m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  s = 16L, training = "oracle", row_ids = d$row_id,
  return = c("W", "dx", "nuisance")
)
```

The wrapper constructs the augmented contrast for each response \(R=Y,D\):

\[
\phi_R=m_{R,1}-m_{R,0}
 +\frac A e(R-m_{R,1})
 -\frac{1-A}{1-e}(R-m_{R,0}).
\]

It then solves the affine equation
\(\sum_iw_i(x)(\theta\phi_{D,i}-\phi_{Y,i})=0\). The
result is a ratio of weighted averages, with common weights for both
signals. Do not average observation-level signal ratios.

The constructor and generic ratio engine are also available separately:

```{r explicit-composition}
signals <- iv_augmented_signals(
  Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A, e = d$e_oracle,
  m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  row_ids = d$row_id, training = "oracle"
)
ratio <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, numerator = signals$phi_y, denominator = signals$phi_d,
  s = 16L, row_ids = signals$row_ids
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ratio$theta, fit$theta)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(ratio$theta_vcov, fit$theta_vcov)))
```

Both high-level estimators use the same weighting controls as `cate_dnn()`
and `np_dnn()`: `method = "exact"` or `"asymp"`, `1 <= k <= s`, and
`normalize` for asymptotic weights. Exact DNN and `k = 1L` are the defaults.
Supply a deterministic integer `s`, or an existing tuning specification.
Without either, the package's paper-default rule resolves the order.
Covariance requires `s < n`. The same order and weight rule are used after
every deletion and retained by `predict()` and `diagnostics()`.
CATE and CLATE expose single-scale DNN only; the two-scale `np_tdnn()`
regression method has no corresponding justification here.

For example, the generic composition can use asymptotic DNN while retaining
the default single neighbor per subsample:

```{r asymptotic-fit}
approximate <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, numerator = signals$phi_y, denominator = signals$phi_d,
  s = 16L, method = "asymp", k = 1L, normalize = TRUE
)
summary(approximate)$coefficients
```

Availability of a weighting option is a computational contract. Statistical
validity still requires the localization, bias and nuisance conditions for
that choice; it does not extend an exact, single-neighbor theorem automatically.

## Data frames and tibbles

Select all columns explicitly. Tibbles follow the same data-frame path;
there is no formula interface or implicit column guessing.

```{r table-fit}
estimate_from_table <- function(data) {
  clate_dnn(
    data = data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), X0 = targets,
    y_col = "Y", d_col = "D", a_col = "A", e_col = "e_oracle",
    m_y0_col = "m_y0_oracle", m_y1_col = "m_y1_oracle",
    m_d0_col = "m_d0_oracle", m_d1_col = "m_d1_oracle",
    s = 16L, training = "oracle", row_ids = data$row_id
  )
}
table_fit <- estimate_from_table(d)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(table_fit$theta, fit$theta)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(table_fit$component_vcov, fit$component_vcov)))
if (requireNamespace("tibble", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tibble_fit <- estimate_from_table(tibble::as_tibble(d))
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(tibble_fit$theta, fit$theta)))
}
```

Every observation and prediction vector must be finite and aligned in the
same row order. Row IDs must be unique, finite/nonmissing numeric or
nonempty character values. IDs document alignment; the wrapper cannot
detect a separately permuted prediction vector supplied without its own
row map. Align external predictions before passing them.

Instrument propensities must lie in `[0,1]` and are clipped to
`[clip,1-clip]`; the default is `clip = 1e-8`. Raw and used propensities
are retained by the constructor. Treatment predictions must lie in
`[0,1]`; outcome predictions are finite but not automatically capped.
Clipping a propensity does not establish overlap, and clipping predictions
does not bound an unbounded observed outcome.

## Report components with the ratio

```{r component-table}
report <- summary(fit)
knitr::kable(report$coefficients, digits = 4, caption = "Conditional ratio and pointwise inference")
knitr::kable(report$components, digits = 4, caption = "Reduced form and first stage")
knitr::kable(report$status, caption = "Computation status by target")
```

For CLATE, the numerator is the adjusted outcome reduced form and the
denominator is the adjusted treatment first stage. `component_vcov` retains
their full paired covariance. `vcov(fit)` returns ratio variance matrices
on the estimator scale; `theta_omega` multiplies those matrices by `neff`.
Do not divide the returned ratio variance by `neff` again.

```{r diagnostics}
info <- as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit))
fields <- c("target_id", "denominator_se", "denominator_stat",
            "instrument_1_mass", "radius_90", "jk_top1_sq_share")
knitr::kable(info[fields], digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Target", "First-stage SE", "First-stage stat.",
                           "Instrument mass", "Radius (90%)", "Largest share"))
```

These diagnostics describe first-stage variation, instrument support,
physical localization and concentration of fitted uncertainty. `neff`
measures reporting-weight concentration, not the number of compliers.
There is no automatic weak-instrument cutoff or target filtering.

## The same plotting workflow as CATE

The fitted object determines the implementation behind each shared call.
`plot_estimates()`, `plot()` and `ggplot2::autoplot()` use the same
profile, forest and pointrange styles as CATE. The coefficient extractor
`plot_data_estimates()` returns the common tidy table, while
`summary(fit)$coefficients` uses the same six columns as CATE.
Undefined ratios and unavailable Wald bounds remain visible in the tables.

```{r plots, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(plot_estimates(fit, style = "forest"))
  print(plot_overlap(fit, type = "mass"))
  print(plot_influence(fit, targets = 2L))
}
```

The remaining common calls are `plot_weights(fit, type = "profile")`,
`type = "cumulative"` or `"kernel"`, `plot_overlap(fit, type = "propensity")`,
and `plot_dashboard(fit)`. Weight and overlap panels require `W`; the
physical-distance weight view also requires `dx`, so retain both as above.
Plots require optional ggplot2. Dashboards use patchwork when installed and
otherwise return a named list of plots. Unavailable panels are omitted or
replaced by diagnostics using the same policy as CATE.

CLATE overlap panels use **instrument** arms and the instrument propensity,
not treatment uptake. Its influence panel shows the weighted paired score
residual `w * (phi_y - theta * phi_d)`. These are neither individual causal
effects nor jackknife pseudo-values. The latter are separately available
through `return = "pseudo_values"`.

## Tuning sensitivity and candidate views

As for CATE and NP regression, `tuning_mode = "grid"` retains the default
fit and adds common candidate, estimate and diagnostic tables. All candidates
reuse the same signals and frozen ranks. This is a sensitivity analysis;
it does not select an order or justify inference after data-dependent selection.

```{r tuning-grid}
grid_fit <- clate_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = targets, Y = d$Y, D = d$D, A = d$A,
  e = d$e_oracle, m_y0 = d$m_y0_oracle, m_y1 = d$m_y1_oracle,
  m_d0 = d$m_d0_oracle, m_d1 = d$m_d1_oracle,
  tuning_mode = "grid", method = "asymp", training = "oracle",
  return = c("W", "dx")
)
head(grid_fit$tuning_grid$candidates)
views <- candidate_fits(grid_fit)
selected <- candidate_fit(grid_fit, 1L)
summary(selected)$coefficients
```

Candidate views have the same class and reporting methods as a scalar fit,
with paired components and covariance recomputed from cached state. They
retain instrument information for overlap plots and use the candidate order
for prediction. Selecting an infeasible candidate gives an actionable error.
`candidate_fits(fit, ids)` can restrict the list to feasible candidate IDs.

```{r tuning-plots, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(plot_estimates(grid_fit, candidates = "all", style = "pointrange"))
  print(plot_tuning(grid_fit))
}
```

`plot_data_estimates(grid_fit, candidates = "all")`, candidate-aware
`plot_weights()` and `diagnostics()` use the same selection grammar as CATE.
`plot_tuning()` also works from a scalar fit's retained state. Stored grid
fits reuse their stored standard errors; refit with `se = TRUE` if these
were omitted and confidence bounds are needed.

## A selected one-sided model

When the design implies \(D(0)=0\), select `one_sided = TRUE` and omit
`m_d0`, or provide an identically zero vector. The wrapper checks `D <= A`.
That observed check alone does not establish the counterfactual restriction.

For a simple example, specify perfect compliance, \(D(a)=a\), and a
constant effect. Here the first-stage signal is identically one and the
estimate and covariance reduce to CATE.

```{r one-sided}
set.seed(320)
n <- 32L
one_X <- matrix(seq(-1, 1, length.out = n), ncol = 1)
A <- rbinom(n, 1, .5)
baseline <- .2 * one_X[, 1]
Y <- baseline + .5 * A + rnorm(n, sd = .1)
one <- clate_dnn(
  X = one_X, x0 = 0, Y = Y, D = A, A = A, e = rep(.5, n),
  m_y0 = baseline, m_y1 = baseline + .5, m_d1 = rep(1, n),
  one_sided = TRUE, s = 6L, training = "oracle", return = "signals"
)
one$components
stopifnot(all(one$signals[, 2] == 1))
```

In general one-sided models, an eligible nonparticipant's augmented
first-stage signal can be negative. The implementation preserves it.

## New reporting profiles

`predict()` changes only the reporting profiles. It reuses the original
observations, frozen signals, metric and resolved order; it fits no nuisance
functions and does not predict outcomes for new households.

```{r new-targets}
predict(fit, X0 = rbind(c(.4, .4), c(.6, .6)), se.fit = TRUE)
predict(table_fit, newdata = data.frame(X1 = .5, X2 = .5), interval = "confidence")
```

## Undefined ratios remain visible

An exactly zero aggregate denominator gives an undefined ratio, while
preserving the components and their covariance. This is different from a
finite negative denominator, which remains a computed signed ratio.

```{r zero-denominator}
zero <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = matrix(1:4), x0 = 0, numerator = c(2, 1, 4, 3),
  denominator = rep(0, 4), s = 2
)
zero$components
zero$status
confint(zero)
ratio_confidence_set(zero$components, zero$component_vcov)
```

For the covariance derivation, exact worked arrays, confidence-set geometry
and pointwise inference conditions, continue with [Paired frozen-score
inference](conditional-late-inference.html). Full-sample inference needs
learner accuracy and deletion stability as well as orthogonality and
undersmoothing. The software's numerical statuses do not certify those
conditions or causal validity. The existing [local IV-GMM
workflow](local-iv-estimation.html) uses a different moment and covariance
route; it is not an alias for this augmented CLATE estimator.
